common_name: Bayou Sunbeam Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Yellow Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bayou Sunbeam is a widely admired Louisiana iris cultivar bearing heavily ruffled, clear yellow flowers with a bright signal on the falls, produced in abundance on well-branched stalks in mid-spring. It has proven to be a vigorous, reliable grower and parent plant in Louisiana iris breeding, and remains popular in Gulf South gardens for the sunny color it brings to pond edges and moist borders. Keep the planting consistently damp through the growing season and top-dress with compost each spring; divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Marie Caillet Louisiana Iris (Orchid-Pink Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Marie Caillet is a historically important Louisiana iris cultivar named for one of the founding figures of organized Louisiana iris breeding, bearing large, softly ruffled orchid-pink flowers that helped establish pink as a serious color class within the group. It remains a garden-worthy performer as well as a notable parent behind many modern pink and lavender Louisiana iris introductions. Keep soil consistently damp through spring bloom and the growing season, feed lightly in early spring, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to sustain strong flowering.

common_name: Frank Chowning Louisiana Iris (Wine-Red Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Frank Chowning is a classic Louisiana iris cultivar named for one of the influential Arkansas hybridizers who helped popularize the group in home gardens, bearing rich wine-red to rosy-red flowers on sturdy, well-branched stalks in mid-spring. Its saturated color and dependable vigor have kept it a garden favorite for decades among heirloom Louisiana iris collections. Keep the bed consistently moist through the growing season, top-dress with compost in early spring, and divide overcrowded clumps every four to five years in late summer to keep the planting blooming well.

common_name: Professor Ike Louisiana Iris (Historic Red Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Professor Ike is one of the historic named Louisiana iris cultivars still grown for its rich red flowers, which helped define red as one of the classic color classes within this group of Gulf South native iris. It is a vigorous, easy-to-grow heirloom well suited to naturalizing along a pond edge or in a consistently damp border. Keep the soil evenly moist through spring bloom and the rest of the growing season, feed lightly in early spring, and divide crowded clumps every four to five years in late summer to keep the clump vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Dixie Deb Louisiana Iris (Classic Early Yellow Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Dixie Deb was one of the first widely popular clear yellow Louisiana iris cultivars and remains a garden standard for its dependable, floriferous performance and compact, early-blooming habit that often opens ahead of many other Louisiana iris cultivars in spring. Its long garden history and easy vigor have kept it in circulation among heirloom iris growers for decades. Keep the bed consistently damp through the growing season, top-dress with compost in early spring, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain strong bloom.
